title: Functions and recursion
short: def, return, defaults, inner helpers, and a free memo with @cache.
what: def gives a block of code a name and inputs; return hands a value back. A function can live inside another and use its variables, which is how most interview recursion is written. @cache remembers answers so repeated calls are free.
analogy: A recipe you can follow from inside another recipe. Write the result of each sub-recipe on a sticky note, and the next time it comes up you read the note instead of cooking again.

frames.label: call stack
frames.say: climb(4) defines ways inside it and calls ways(4). The call gets a frame on the stack with its own k = 4.

frames.label: call stack
frames.say: ways(4) needs ways(3) first, which needs ways(2). Each call waits on top of the one that called it.

frames.label: call stack
frames.say: The chain reaches ways(0), the base case: it returns 1 without calling anything. Its frame is popped.

frames.label: call stack
frames.say: Back up: ways(1) = 1, then ways(2) = ways(1) + ways(0) = 2. @cache stores each answer as it returns.

frames.label: call stack
frames.say: ways(3) = ways(2) + ways(1) = 3. ways(1) came straight from the cache, so no new frames.

frames.label: call stack
frames.say: ways(4) still needs ways(2). The cache returns 2 at once instead of redoing that whole branch.

frames.label: call stack
frames.say: ways(4) = 3 + 2 = 5. nonlocal calls lets ways add to the outer counter: only 6 calls in total.

frames.label: without setrecursionlimit
frames.say: climb(3000) nests 3000 calls. Python stops near 1000 with RecursionError, so the code raises the limit first.

when: Same smaller problem inside the problem
Walk a tree or a grid with DFS
Recursion that repeats the same calls
A helper that updates an outer answer
watch: Without nonlocal, calls += 1 inside the inner function raises UnboundLocalError.
@cache needs hashable arguments: pass tuples, not lists.
Deep recursion hits the 1000 limit. Call sys.setrecursionlimit, or rewrite it as a loop.
